title: The Count of Monte Cristo, Part 2
author: Alexandre Dumas
summary: Na primeira parte, Edmond Dantès foi traído, passou catorze anos preso no Castelo de If, fugiu e encontrou um tesouro fabuloso. Agora, anos depois, um homem misterioso e riquíssimo, o Conde de Monte Cristo, chega a Paris e entra na vida elegante dos homens que o destruíram: Fernand, Danglars e Villefort. Entre bailes, segredos antigos e planos pacientes, ele reencontra Mercedes e conhece os filhos dos seus inimigos, e a vingança começa a se tornar mais complicada do que ele imaginava.

chapters.title: A Stranger in Paris
paragraphs: In the spring of 1838, everyone in the elegant salons of Paris was talking about one man: the Count of Monte Cristo. Nobody knew where he came from. Some said he was Italian, others said he was Maltese or Greek. He was pale, with black hair and dark, burning eyes, and he seemed to be fantastically rich.

It was a young man called Albert de Morcerf who brought him to Paris. During the carnival in Rome, Albert had been captured by Luigi Vampa, a famous bandit. The bandits wanted a huge ransom, and they were ready to kill him. But the Count went alone to their hiding place in the old catacombs, spoke a few words to Vampa, and Albert was free.
“You saved my life,” Albert told him. “How can I thank you?”
“You can introduce me to Parisian society,” said the Count with a smile. “I have never been to Paris.”

So, on the morning of the 21st of May, at exactly half past ten, the Count arrived at Albert’s house for breakfast. Albert’s friends were waiting, curious to meet this strange man. Among them was a young army officer, Maximilien Morrel.
When the Count heard his name, something changed in his eyes. “Morrel? Is your father the shipowner from Marseille?”
“Yes, he was. He is dead now. He died happy, because a stranger saved our family. We never discovered who it was. My sister keeps the red purse like a holy object.”
The Count turned away for a moment. When he looked back, his face was calm again. “I hope we will be friends, Monsieur Morrel.”

After breakfast, Albert took the Count to meet his parents. His father, the Count de Morcerf, was a general and a member of the Chamber of Peers. He was tall and proud, with a military moustache. The Count bowed politely. He recognised him at once. It was Fernand Mondego, the fisherman from the Catalans.
Then Albert’s mother came into the room. She was still very beautiful, with black hair and dark eyes, but her face was sad. When she saw the Count, she went pale and held on to the door.
“Are you unwell, Mother?” Albert asked.
“No, it is nothing,” said Mercédès. “Monsieur, you saved my son’s life. I will always be grateful.”
The Count bowed again. His voice was cold and polite, but inside he was shaking. He had not seen her for twenty-three years.
“Will you stay for dinner?” Mercédès asked.
“Thank you, madame, but I have another appointment.”
When he had gone, Mercédès sat alone for a long time. “It is impossible,” she whispered. “And yet… that voice.”

The Count drove back to the magnificent house he had bought on the Champs-Élysées. Waiting for him there was a beautiful young Greek woman named Haydée, the daughter of a pasha. He had bought her freedom from a slave market years before, and now she lived in his house like a princess.
“Have you seen him, my lord?” she asked.
“I have seen him, Haydée. Be patient. Very soon, the whole of Paris will hear your story.”

chapters.title: The Banker and the Prosecutor
paragraphs: A few days later, the Count went to visit the Baron Danglars, one of the richest bankers in Paris. Danglars was now fat and grey, with small, greedy eyes. His house was full of expensive and ugly things.
“Monsieur le Comte,” said Danglars, “I have received a letter from the bank of Thomson and French. They say I must give you unlimited credit. Unlimited! I don’t understand. What does it mean?”
“It means exactly what it says,” answered the Count calmly. “I may need a lot of money. For example, I may need a million this week.”
Danglars almost dropped his glasses. “A million? But… of course, Monsieur le Comte. Whatever you need.”

The Count then met Madame Danglars, an elegant woman who loved to gamble on the stock exchange, and their daughter Eugénie, who was engaged to Albert de Morcerf. Neither Albert nor Eugénie was very excited about the marriage.

The third enemy was the most powerful of all. Gérard de Villefort was now the King’s Prosecutor in Paris, a cold, severe man who was famous for sending criminals to the scaffold. The Count went to his house and talked to him about justice.
“Human justice is weak,” said the Count. “But I believe that some men are sent by God to reward and to punish.”
Villefort looked at him strangely. “You speak as if you were one of those men.”
“Perhaps I am,” said the Count, and smiled.

Then the Count bought a country house at Auteuil, just outside Paris. His servant Bertuccio, a Corsican, became very pale when he saw it. “Sir, please, not this house! Something terrible happened here.”
“Tell me,” said the Count, although he already knew the story.

“Years ago, Villefort had a secret lover in this house. She was married to another man. She had a baby, and Villefort wanted to hide it. One night I saw him bury a box in the garden. I attacked him with my knife, because I hated him for other reasons. I thought I had killed him, and I dug up the box. Inside there was a baby, and it was still alive! I took it to a hospital. Later my sister adopted the boy. We called him Benedetto. But he grew up to be a thief and a criminal.”
“And who was the woman?” asked the Count.
“I found out later. She is now Madame Danglars.”
The Count invited many guests to dinner at Auteuil. Danglars and his wife came, and Villefort, and several other people. After dinner, the Count took them into the garden.

“Gentlemen,” he said lightly, “this house has a strange history. When my workers were digging in the garden, they found a small box with the bones of a baby inside. I think a crime was committed here.”
Madame Danglars almost fainted. Villefort went white and held on to a tree. Later he whispered to her, “He knows. I don’t know how, but that man knows everything.”

Among the guests was a young man who called himself Prince Andrea Cavalcanti, a rich Italian nobleman. The Count had introduced him to Danglars, and Danglars was already thinking that this prince would be a much better husband for Eugénie than Albert. But the young man was not a prince at all. He was Benedetto, Villefort’s lost son.

chapters.title: Valentine and Maximilien
paragraphs: In the garden of Villefort’s house, behind a tall wooden gate, a young woman and a young man were talking in whispers. The young woman was Valentine de Villefort, the prosecutor’s daughter from his first marriage. She was gentle and pretty, with fair hair and blue eyes. The young man on the other side of the gate was Maximilien Morrel.
“My father wants me to marry Baron Franz d’Épinay,” said Valentine sadly. “I don’t love him. I love you, Maximilien. But my father will never agree. He is so proud.”
“Then run away with me,” said Maximilien.
“I can’t. I can’t leave my grandfather. He has nobody else.”

Her grandfather was Monsieur Noirtier, the old Bonapartist. He was now completely paralysed. He could not move or speak. He could only move his eyes. But his mind was as clear as ever, and Valentine understood him perfectly. When he closed his eyes once, it meant yes. When he blinked many times, it meant no.

Villefort’s second wife, Héloïse, had a young son, Édouard, a spoiled and cruel little boy. Madame de Villefort was always very sweet to Valentine, but in secret she was jealous. Valentine was going to inherit a lot of money from her mother’s family and from her grandfather. Madame de Villefort wanted all that money for her own son.
One day, Madame de Villefort met the Count in a salon. She was very interested in chemistry. “They say you know a lot about poisons, Monsieur le Comte,” she said.

“A little,” said the Count. “There are poisons in the East that kill slowly, without leaving a trace. A doctor would think the victim died of a natural illness. Of course, every poison has an antidote. Brucine, for example, is a medicine in small doses. In large doses, it kills.”
She listened with great attention. The Count watched her face and understood what was in her mind. He did not stop her.

Soon after this, terrible things began to happen in Villefort’s house. First Valentine’s grandmother, Madame de Saint-Méran, died suddenly. Then an old servant, Barrois, drank a glass of lemonade from Noirtier’s room and died in terrible pain.
The family doctor, Monsieur d’Avrigny, took Villefort aside. “Someone in this house is using poison,” he said quietly. “I am sure of it. And who gains from these deaths? Your daughter Valentine.”
“Valentine? Impossible!” said Villefort. But he began to look at his gentle daughter with fear.

Old Noirtier, however, knew the truth. He had seen everything from his chair. He could not speak, but he did something to protect Valentine. He changed his will and made it impossible for her to marry Franz. And every day he gave her a little of his own medicine, which contained brucine. Slowly, her body became used to the poison.
One night, Maximilien came to the Count’s house in despair. “Valentine is sick! She is dying, and nobody believes she is being poisoned. You are so powerful. You can do anything. Please help me!”
The Count was shocked. “Valentine? Villefort’s daughter? You love her?”
“More than my life.”

For a moment the Count was silent. He had let this crime begin, because he wanted Villefort’s house to be destroyed. Now the son of his old friend Morrel was going to lose everything he loved. The Count put his hand on Maximilien’s shoulder.
“Go home and wait. Do not despair. I promise you, Valentine will live.”

chapters.title: What Happened at Janina
paragraphs: One morning, a short article appeared in a Paris newspaper. It came from Janina, a city in Greece. The article said that a French officer called Fernand, who had served the Pasha Ali Tebelin, had betrayed his master. He had sold the castle to the Turks for money. The pasha had been killed, and his wife and daughter had been sold as slaves.
Everyone in Paris knew that the Count de Morcerf had once served Ali Pasha, and that his name was Fernand. The Chamber of Peers decided to investigate.
Fernand stood in front of the other peers. He spoke confidently. “Gentlemen, these are lies. I was loyal to Ali Pasha until the end. All the witnesses are dead.”
At that moment, the president of the Chamber said, “A witness has asked to speak.”
A young woman came in. She was dressed in Greek clothes, and her face was covered with a veil. She lifted the veil. It was Haydée.

“I am Haydée, the daughter of Ali Tebelin, Pasha of Janina,” she said in a clear voice. “I was four years old when my father died. I was there. I saw everything.” She told them how a French officer had promised to protect her family, and how he had opened the doors of the castle to the enemy. “My mother and I were sold to a slave merchant. My mother died of grief. And this is the man who sold us.” She pointed at Fernand. “I have the documents here, with his signature.”

Fernand looked at her with horror. He tried to speak, but no words came. Then he turned and ran out of the room. The Chamber declared him guilty of treason. In one day, the proud general had lost his honour.
Albert was in despair. “Who did this to my father? Who sent that article to the newspaper?”

His friend Beauchamp, a journalist, investigated. “The information came from Danglars, the banker. But Danglars says he only asked for information after the Count of Monte Cristo spoke to him about Janina. And that Greek woman lives in the Count’s house.”
Albert’s face became red with anger. “The Count! The man I called my friend! He planned all this. I will make him pay.”
That evening the Count was at the opera. Albert came into his box in front of everyone. “Monsieur,” he said loudly, “you have destroyed my father’s honour. Tomorrow we will fight a duel.”
The Count looked at him calmly. “Very well. Tomorrow at eight o’clock, with pistols. And I warn you, I never miss.”

chapters.title: Mercédès
paragraphs: That night, the Count was sitting alone in his study, cleaning his pistols. A servant came in. “Sir, a lady wishes to see you. She is wearing a veil.”
The lady came in and lifted her veil. It was Mercédès. She looked at him for a long moment, and then she said one word.
“Edmond.”
The Count did not move. “Madame, you are mistaken. My name is…”
“No,” she said. “I knew you the first time I heard your voice. Edmond, you are going to kill my son.”

The Count’s face became hard. “Madame, your husband destroyed my life. Do you know how I disappeared? Fernand and Danglars wrote a letter that sent me to prison. Fernand posted it with his own hand.” He took an old, yellow piece of paper from a box. It was the letter from the tavern. He had found it in the prison records. “I spent fourteen years in a dark cell. My father died of hunger. And you married the man who did this.”

Mercédès read the letter, and she began to cry. “I didn’t know. I swear I didn’t know. I waited for you, Edmond. Everyone said you were dead. My heart was dead too. But Albert is innocent. Don’t punish the son for the father’s crime. You are good, Edmond. I know you are still good.”
The Count was silent for a long time. Then he said in a broken voice, “Your son will live, Mercédès.”
“Thank you!” She took his hands. “And you? Will you let him kill you?”
“I will not shoot at him. Tomorrow I will die.” He smiled sadly. “I have built my plan for ten years, and one word from you has destroyed it.”
But the next morning, something unexpected happened. Albert arrived at the place of the duel, pale and serious. He had spoken to his mother during the night, and she had told him the whole story.

“Monsieur le Comte,” said Albert in front of all the witnesses, “I was wrong. You had the right to punish my father for what he did to you. I ask you to forgive me. I hope you will accept my hand in friendship.”
The Count, deeply moved, took his hand. Everyone was amazed.
When Fernand heard what had happened, he was furious. He went to the Count’s house himself. “My son is a coward! But I am not. Who are you? What is your real name?”
The Count went into the next room. When he came back, he was wearing a sailor’s jacket and a sailor’s hat, as he had worn twenty-three years before.
“Fernand,” he said quietly, “do you remember me now? I am Edmond Dantès, the man whose fiancée you stole on the day of his wedding.”

Fernand gave a terrible cry and ran out of the house. He went home and stood at the bottom of the stairs. He saw his wife and son coming down with small bags in their hands. They were leaving the house forever. They took nothing, not even his money, because they did not want anything that had come from his crimes. They walked past him without seeing him.
A moment later, as their carriage drove away, a pistol shot was heard from Fernand’s room. The Count de Morcerf was dead.
Mercédès went back to Marseille, to the little house where old Dantès had lived. Albert joined the army and sailed to Africa as a simple soldier, to build a new and honest name for himself.

chapters.title: A Death in the House of Villefort
paragraphs: The Count kept his promise to Maximilien. He bought the house next to Villefort’s, and he made a secret door in the wall behind Valentine’s bed. Every night he sat there in the dark and watched over her.
One night Valentine woke up and saw a man standing beside her bed. She almost screamed.

“Don’t be afraid,” said the Count gently. “I am a friend of Maximilien. I have been watching over you for four nights. Every night someone comes into your room and puts poison in your glass of water. Every night I pour it away and put a medicine in its place.”
“Who is it?” whispered Valentine. “Who wants to kill me?”
“Stay here and watch. Pretend to sleep.”

Valentine closed her eyes. After a while, the door opened softly. Someone came in, poured something into her glass and went out again. In the light of the lamp, Valentine saw the face. It was her stepmother, Madame de Villefort.

The Count came back. “Now you know. Listen to me, Valentine. If you want to live, and if you want to marry Maximilien, you must trust me completely. Will you do whatever I ask, even if it is frightening?”
“Yes,” she said. “I trust you.”
He gave her a small green pill. “Take this. Whatever happens, don’t be afraid. When you wake up, you will be safe.”
She swallowed the pill and fell into a deep sleep. Her hands became cold, and her heart seemed to stop.

The next morning, the nurse screamed. Valentine was lying on the bed, pale and still. The doctor examined her and shook his head. “She is dead,” he said. Villefort fell to his knees beside the bed. Old Noirtier sat in his chair, and tears ran from his eyes.
Maximilien heard the news and ran to the house. When he saw Valentine on the bed, he almost went mad. “She was murdered!” he shouted. “And I will find the murderer!”
Valentine was buried in the cemetery of Père-Lachaise. After the funeral, the Count found Maximilien alone beside the grave. The young man had a pistol in his pocket.
“Maximilien,” said the Count. “What are you going to do?”
“I am going to join her. Leave me alone.”

The Count took the pistol from him. “Listen to me. I am the man who saved your father with a red purse. I am Edmond Dantès. Your father loved me when everyone else forgot me. Now I ask you one thing. Wait one month. Live for one month. If at the end of that time you still want to die, I will help you myself. I promise.”
Maximilien looked at him for a long time. Then he gave him his hand. “One month. On the fifth of October.”
“On the fifth of October,” said the Count, “come to the island of Monte Cristo.”

chapters.title: The Prosecutor’s Last Trial
paragraphs: Meanwhile, the false prince Andrea Cavalcanti had been arrested. On the night of his engagement to Eugénie Danglars, the police came to the party. He was wanted for murder. Months before, an old enemy from his days in prison had found him in Paris and asked him for money. That man was Caderousse. The two of them had tried to rob the Count’s house together, and when Caderousse climbed out of the window, Andrea had stabbed him. Before Caderousse died, the Count had shown him his true face. “Edmond Dantès!” Caderousse had whispered, and he died asking God for forgiveness.
Eugénie did not cry when the engagement was broken. She cut her hair, put on men’s clothes and left Paris with her friend to become a singer. She had never wanted to marry anybody.
The trial of Andrea Cavalcanti was the most exciting event in Paris. The courtroom was full. Villefort himself was the prosecutor. He had not slept for days, but he was determined to do his job.
That morning, before he left for court, Villefort went to his wife’s room. He looked at her coldly. “Madame, where do you keep the poison that you have been using?”
She went white. “I… I don’t understand.”

“You have killed my wife’s mother, the servant Barrois and my daughter Valentine. I know everything. I will not send you to the scaffold, because that would shame my name. But when I come back from court this afternoon, I don’t want to find you alive.”
Then he went to court. The judge asked the prisoner, “What is your name?”

Andrea stood up and smiled. “I don’t know my name. But I know my father’s name. I was born at number 28, Rue de la Fontaine, in Auteuil, on the night of the 27th of September 1817. My father buried me alive in the garden. My father is the King’s Prosecutor, Monsieur de Villefort!”
The courtroom exploded with noise. Everyone looked at Villefort. He stood up slowly. His face was grey.
“It is true,” he said in a strange, quiet voice. “I am guilty. Gentlemen, I will place myself in the hands of my successor.” And he walked out of the court like a man in a dream.

In his carriage, a terrible thought came to him. “My wife! I told her to die. But I am a criminal too. I have no right to judge her. We will go away together, with our son.” He shouted to the driver to go faster.
He ran up the stairs of his house. “Héloïse!” She was lying on the floor of her room. She had taken the poison. And on the sofa, he saw his little son Édouard. The boy was not moving.
“I could not leave him without a mother,” said a weak voice. They were her last words.
Villefort ran out of the room, crying wildly. At that moment the Count of Monte Cristo arrived. “Villefort,” he said, “do you remember Edmond Dantès? I am Edmond Dantès. Now we are even.”
Villefort took him by the arm and pulled him into the room. “Look!” he screamed. “Look at what your revenge has done! My son! My son!”

The Count looked at the dead child, and his face changed. He tried to bring the boy back to life, but it was too late. When he came out of the room, his face was white. Behind him, Villefort was in the garden, digging in the ground with his hands. “I will find him,” he said. “I know he is here. I will find my child.” Villefort had lost his mind.
The Count walked away slowly. For the first time, he asked himself a terrible question. “Have I gone too far? Was God really guiding my hand?”

chapters.title: The Banker’s Hunger
paragraphs: The last enemy was Danglars. For months, the Count had been working silently against him. He had used his telegraph contacts to send false news, and Danglars had lost huge sums of money on the stock exchange. Then several banks failed, and Danglars lost even more. His wife left him. His daughter had run away. All he had left was the five million francs that a charity hospital had deposited in his bank.
Danglars took the hospital’s money and ran away to Italy in a coach. He planned to start a new life with a new name.
But near Rome, the coach stopped in the middle of the night. Armed men surrounded it. “Get out,” said a voice. It was the bandit Luigi Vampa.
The bandits took Danglars to the catacombs and locked him in a small cell. They did not hurt him. They did not even search him. But they did not give him any food.
After many hours, Danglars was very hungry. He called a guard who was eating a big piece of chicken. “I would like to eat something too.”
“Of course, sir. What would you like? We have everything.”
“A chicken, please.”
“Certainly. That will be one hundred thousand francs.”
“A hundred thousand francs for a chicken? Are you mad?”
“That is the price here, sir.”

Danglars refused. But the next day he was even hungrier, and he paid. Then he had to pay for bread, and for water, at the same terrible prices. Day after day, his money disappeared. After twelve days, he had only fifty thousand francs left.

He was thin, weak and terrified. He lay on the floor of his cell and thought about his life. For the first time, he thought about the people he had hurt. He remembered a young sailor who had once been happy, and a letter written with his left hand.
“Please,” he cried at last. “Take the rest of my money. Only let me live. I don’t want to die of hunger.”
A tall man in a black cloak came into the cell. “Do you repent?” he asked.
“Yes! Yes, I repent!”

“Then I forgive you,” said the man. He stepped into the light. It was the Count of Monte Cristo. “I am the man you sent to prison. Edmond Dantès. You are suffering from hunger, but my old father died of it because of you. Still, I forgive you, because I also need forgiveness. Keep your fifty thousand francs. The money you stole from the hospital has been returned. Now you are free.”
The bandits gave Danglars a good meal and left him by the side of a road. In the morning, he bent down to drink from a stream. He saw his face in the water. His hair had turned completely white.

chapters.title: Wait and Hope
paragraphs: Before the fifth of October, the Count went back to Marseille with Maximilien. There he went to visit Mercédès in the little house where old Dantès had once lived. She was dressed in black, and her hair had begun to turn grey.
“Edmond,” she said, “I have no more tears. I pray for Albert, and I pray for you. Will you forgive me?”
“There is nothing to forgive,” said the Count. “You were weak, and I was hard. We have both suffered.”
“Goodbye, Edmond. I will stay here, near the sea, and wait for my son.”

Then the Count took a boat to the Château d’If. The prison was now empty and open to visitors. A guide showed him the dark cells. “This is where a terrible prisoner, Edmond Dantès, lived,” said the guide. “And this is the cell of a mad priest who believed in a treasure. They say the young man escaped in a sack, but he drowned.” The guide gave him some old pieces of linen, covered with fine writing. They were pages of Faria’s book. The Count held them in his hands and felt that his old friend was speaking to him. “God has helped me to punish the guilty,” he thought. “But I must not try to be God myself.”

On the fifth of October, a small boat brought Maximilien to the island of Monte Cristo. The Count was waiting for him on the rocks. He led him down into a cave, which was now a magnificent room full of soft lights and flowers.
“The month is over,” said Maximilien. “Do you still want me to live?”
“Are you still so unhappy?”
“Yes. I only want to die.”
“Then I will keep my promise,” said the Count. He gave him a small cup with a green paste. “This will make you sleep, and you will feel no pain.”

Maximilien took the cup and swallowed the paste without hesitating. He sat down and closed his eyes. Slowly, the room seemed to become darker. Through the darkness, he saw a door open. A woman in white came into the room. It was Valentine. She looked like an angel, and she was smiling.
“Valentine!” he whispered. “Am I in heaven?”

But it was not heaven. The paste was only a sleeping medicine, like the pill that Valentine had taken. She had not died. The Count had taken her secretly from her grave, and she had been living on the island, with Haydée and old Noirtier, waiting for this moment.
When Maximilien woke up, Valentine was holding his hand. The Count was gone. Jacopo, the Count’s old friend, gave them a letter.

“My dear Maximilien,” it said. “There is a ship for you and Valentine at the shore. All that I have on this island, my house on the Champs-Élysées and my house at Auteuil, I give to you and to her as a wedding present. Live and be happy. There is neither happiness nor unhappiness in this world. There is only the comparison of one state with another. Only a man who has felt the deepest despair can feel the greatest joy. Until the day when God will reveal the future to man, all human wisdom is contained in these two words: wait and hope. Your friend, Edmond Dantès, Count of Monte Cristo.”

Valentine and Maximilien ran to the shore. Far away, on the blue horizon, they saw a white sail moving slowly toward the east. On the deck of the ship, the Count was standing beside Haydée, who held his hand. She had loved him for a long time, and at last he had found the courage to love again.
“Where is he going?” asked Maximilien. “Will we ever see him again?”
Valentine looked at the little white sail until it disappeared. “I don’t know,” she said softly. “Didn’t he just tell us? We must wait and hope.”
